passage:
Playschool note, Thursday (Ms Joyce, Butterfly group)
At drawing time Afreen had the only box of glitter crayons. Jagdish asked first, and she handed him two at once, saying, "You gave me your sticker yesterday." When Bittu reached for one, Afreen covered the box with both arms. "No. You never give me." Bittu sat down hard and sulked. I knelt between them and said, "Afreen remembers who shared. Bittu, what could you share today?" Bittu offered his blue clay. Afreen took it and slid one crayon across 🙂
Next step: a sharing song before drawing tomorrow.

qa.q: What had Jagdish given Afreen yesterday?
qa.a: Jagdish had given Afreen a sticker yesterday.

qa.q: What does Afreen covering the box with both arms show about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she feels Bittu hasn't earned a crayon, because in her mind he never shares with her.

qa.q: Which choice by Ms Joyce turned the moment around?
qa.a: Instead of ordering Afreen to share, Ms Joyce asked Bittu what he could share, and his blue clay opened the way to a crayon.

qa.q: What might it feel like for Bittu to hear "You never give me"?
qa.a: Bittu might feel stung and shut out, which is why he sits down hard and sulks until he finds a way to join in.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child sharing with the friend who shared before and refusing the one who never does.

passage: Behind the rice fields, under the big guava tree, Reena, five, had filled her frock pocket with guavas. Joseph came running. Yesterday he had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond. Reena held out the biggest guava straight away. "For you. You gave me." Then Kuttan came, the boy who always kept his mango slices behind his back. "Give me one." Reena shook her head hard. "You don't give. I don't give." Kuttan kicked at the mud. Reena's Ammachi, drying chillies on a mat nearby, called out, "Kuttan, bring your mango tomorrow, and see what happens."

qa.q: What did Joseph share with Reena yesterday?
qa.a: He had split his tamarind pod with her at the pond.

qa.q: Why did Reena shake her head hard at Kuttan?
qa.a: In her mind Kuttan never shares, so he hadn't earned a guava: "You don't give. I don't give."

qa.q: What does Ammachi's suggestion offer Kuttan, and why might it work?
qa.a: It gives Kuttan a way to earn a turn by bringing his mango tomorrow, which fits the way Reena thinks about fairness 🙂

qa.q: How might Kuttan feel watching Joseph get the biggest guava?
qa.a: Kuttan might feel left out and cross, and perhaps start to notice that hiding his mango has a cost.

grounding: A young child gives her best guava to the friend who shared with her and refuses the boy who never shares.

passage: In the small park near their flats in Cape Town, Siddiq, five, was pushing his new red digger through the sand. Thabo wandered over. Last Saturday Thabo had let Siddiq ride Thabo's scooter all the way to the bench and back. "You can dig," Siddiq said, handing over the digger. Then Oliver from the swings came close, the boy who never let anyone touch his bucket. "My turn." Siddiq put a hand on the digger's scoop. "No. Thabo's turn. You never share your bucket." Oliver's face crumpled. On the bench, Siddiq's dad leaned forward. "What if Oliver lends the bucket?" Siddiq thought about it for a long time.

qa.q: What had Thabo let Siddiq ride last Saturday?
qa.a: Thabo had let Siddiq ride Thabo's scooter all the way to the bench and back.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq hand the digger to Thabo so quickly?
qa.a: He remembered the scooter ride and felt Thabo deserved a turn back, like a fair swap.

qa.q: Was Dad's question a good way to handle the moment, and why?
qa.a: Yes; instead of forcing Siddiq to share, Dad offered Oliver a way into the "you give, I give" deal that Siddiq already believes in.

qa.q: How might Oliver see Siddiq's "You never share your bucket"?
qa.a: Oliver may feel hurt and surprised, perhaps realising for the first time that other children remember when he doesn't share.

grounding: A young child lends his toy to the friend who shared a scooter with him and refuses the child who never shares.

passage:
Monday. In the back of his rough notebook, Lokesh, ten, kept a list: Baljeet lent eraser (2 times). Me helped Baljeet with maps (1). Ritu owes me a pencil.
Wednesday. After the class clean-up, Sir handed out laddoos: three for Lokesh, "my best helper", and one for Baljeet. Lokesh's face went red. "That's not fair! Baljeet carried six chairs, I carried four. He should get more!" The class stared. Sir blinked. "Lokesh, it's a laddoo." "It's the rule," Lokesh said, and pushed one across the desk.
Saturday. Baljeet saw the list while copying homework. "You count everything?" Lokesh shrugged, cheeks hot. "Someone has to." Baljeet laughed and crossed out "eraser (2)". "Keep your list. I don't need a bill."

qa.q: How many chairs did Baljeet carry, according to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh said Baljeet carried six chairs and Lokesh carried four.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh's face go red when he got three laddoos?
qa.a: By his count Baljeet had worked harder, so the split felt unfair to him, even though he was the one getting extra.

qa.q: Lokesh pushed a laddoo across. What could he try next time a split feels wrong?
qa.a: He could raise it quietly with Sir instead of shouting it in front of the class, keeping the fairness without the scene.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel on finding himself listed in Lokesh's notebook?
qa.a: Baljeet seems amused rather than hurt, and wants to show Lokesh that their friendship doesn't need keeping count.

grounding: Across a week, a child keeps a tally of favours and loudly objects to a split that favours himself, showing an early, rigid sense of fairness.

passage: Jomon, you're counting the chocolates again, I can see your lips moving. Come here, mone. When your Seema aunty was nine, I was worse. I kept a tally on the kitchen wall with charcoal: who pumped water, who fed the hens, who helped whom with sums. One day my father cut a jackfruit and gave me the biggest share because I had swept the yard. I shouted, "No! Thomas pumped water twice, he gets more!" Everyone laughed, and my father said, "Seema, just eat." I wouldn't touch it until Thomas had the bigger piece. I was right about fairness, mind you. But I was so busy counting that I never enjoyed a single bite. Share them, mone, and don't keep a wall.

qa.q: Where did young Seema keep her tally?
qa.a: On the kitchen wall, with charcoal.

qa.q: Why wouldn't young Seema touch her jackfruit?
qa.a: She felt the split was unfair because Thomas had pumped water twice, and she couldn't enjoy extra she felt she hadn't earned.

qa.q: What is Seema aunty hoping Jomon will choose with the chocolates?
qa.a: She hopes Jomon will share them freely rather than counting every piece, keeping fairness without letting the tally spoil the fun.

qa.q: How might Thomas have felt when young Seema shouted that he should get more?
qa.a: Thomas may have been surprised and a bit embarrassed by the fuss, but perhaps pleased that his work was noticed.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a child, she kept a tally of chores and refused a bigger share that was meant for her, fairness held rigidly.

passage: The school fair closed in five minutes, the lights were going off one by one, and the lemonade stall's tin was full of sticky coins. "Quick, just grab and go," said Pallavi, pushing a bigger heap towards Himani. "You made the sign." "No!" Himani's voice rang across the ground. "You squeezed forty lemons. I only squeezed twelve. And Mehak washed all the cups. We count it properly." The watchman was already rattling his keys at the gate. Pallavi groaned. Himani knelt on the grass, sorting coins by torchlight: one pile for squeezing, one for cups, one for the sign. Her own pile came out smallest. She nodded, satisfied, just as the gate clanged.

qa.q: How many lemons did Pallavi squeeze, according to Himani?
qa.a: Himani said Pallavi squeezed forty lemons.

qa.q: Why did Himani look satisfied even though her own pile came out smallest?
qa.a: What mattered to her was that each pile matched the work done; a fair count felt better than extra coins.

qa.q: With the gate closing, what could Himani have chosen instead of sorting every coin?
qa.a: She could have taken the tin home and split it properly next day, keeping fairness without keeping everyone waiting in the dark.

qa.q: What is it like for Pallavi to have a generous offer turned down so loudly?
qa.a: Pallavi may feel frustrated and a little embarrassed, since the bigger heap was meant kindly and she just wanted to go home.

grounding: A child insists loudly on an exact split of stall money by effort, even though it leaves her with less, showing a rigid sense of fairness.

passage:
Friday
Tarun lent me his chemistry notes again. That's the whole of Unit 4 now, plus the night he explained moles to me on the phone at 10 pm. I keep thinking: what have I given him back? Nothing. I bought him a cold drink once. That doesn't count.
Today he asked if I could film his cricket trial on Sunday. Of course I said yes, right away, even though Sunday is my cousin's engagement. I'll just go late.
The weird part: at lunch he joked, "You owe me like ten pizzas, Nilesh." Everyone laughed. I laughed. But something went tight in my chest, like there's a bill growing that I can never clear. I don't want to feel like that about my best friend.

qa.q: Which unit's chemistry notes has Tarun lent?
qa.a: Tarun has lent the whole of Unit 4.

qa.q: What made something go tight in Nilesh's chest at lunch?
qa.a: Tarun's joke about owing ten pizzas made the help feel like a growing bill that Nilesh can never clear 😔

qa.q: Nilesh said yes to Sunday straight away, despite the engagement. What might have been a better choice?
qa.a: Nilesh could have offered another time; saying yes out of guilt, at a cost to family, turns friendship into a ledger.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel if he knew his pizza joke landed so heavily?
qa.a: Tarun would probably be surprised and sorry, since he likely meant it as teasing between best friends, not a real debt.

grounding: A teenager who has received a friend's notes and help feels guilty about not repaying, and senses the friendship turning into a ledger.

passage: All through the board exams, Ramesh had lent Jatin his bicycle, walking the three kilometres to the kasba school himself so Jatin could reach the far exam centre on time. Now the exams were over, and Jatin could not stop thinking about it. Each time he passed Ramesh's courtyard, he felt the bicycle bell ringing somewhere in his chest. So on Sunday he turned up at dawn to help Ramesh's family bring in the wheat. He worked till his palms blistered. At noon Ramesh handed him a tumbler of water and said, "Why are you killing yourself? It was a cycle, not a loan." Jatin didn't know what to say. He only knew that until he'd paid something back, he couldn't quite look Ramesh in the eye.

qa.q: How far did Ramesh walk so Jatin could use the bicycle?
qa.a: Ramesh walked the three kilometres to the kasba school.

qa.q: Why did Jatin work till his palms blistered?
qa.a: He felt he owed Ramesh for the bicycle and couldn't look him in the eye until he'd paid something back.

qa.q: When Ramesh says "It was a cycle, not a loan", what choice does Jatin have?
qa.a: Jatin could accept the gift as freely given, say a real thank-you, and help in future because he wants to rather than to clear a debt.

qa.q: How does Ramesh seem to see the favour?
qa.a: Ramesh sees it as a simple kindness between friends and seems uneasy that Jatin is treating it like a debt.

grounding: A teenager who received a friend's bicycle for the exams feels a strong pull to repay it and cannot rest until he has.

passage: The tanker hadn't come for two days, and the four flatmates in 3B were rationing buckets. Kunal noticed it again that evening: Samir filling his bottle from the drum Kunal and Vikrant had carried up five floors, then settling on the sofa with his phone. It had been like this since June. Samir ate the dal others cooked, borrowed chargers, never took the rubbish down. Nobody had said a word. But things were shifting. Prateek now cooked exactly three portions. Vikrant had stopped offering Samir lifts. In the flat chat, someone posted a photo of the full sink with "guess whose plate". Tonight, when Samir asked, "Any water left for me?", Prateek said, "Plenty. Down on the ground floor." Kunal watched Samir's face and wondered how long before someone said it straight.

qa.q: How many floors did Kunal and Vikrant carry the drum?
qa.a: They carried it up five floors.

qa.q: What is on Kunal's mind while watching Samir's face?
qa.a: Kunal is wondering how long the silent treatment can go on before someone tells Samir straight.

qa.q: What choice would help more now than exact portions and pointed jokes?
qa.a: One flatmate could calmly tell Samir what's been noticed, the water, the dishes, the rubbish, and ask him to share the work before the gossip hardens.

qa.q: What might the last few weeks have felt like from Samir's side?
qa.a: Samir may have noticed fewer lifts and smaller portions without knowing why, so Prateek's comment might land like a sudden slap.

grounding: A flatmate notices one person taking without giving and watches the others withdraw help, gossip and make pointed comments instead of confronting him.

passage: On the first Sunday of every month, the five boys in the Koramangala PG split the grocery bill on a sheet taped to the fridge. Divyansh kept the sheet. For four months, Mohit's line had said "will pay later". He always said it cheerfully, and he always ate the most instant noodles. This month Divyansh noticed that nobody had bought the oat milk Mohit liked. When Mohit asked for a lift to the station, Arun suddenly had "a meeting". At dinner, Chirag held up the last noodle packet and said loudly, "Whoever paid for this gets it." Everyone laughed except Mohit, who went a bit red. "Guys, I'll settle up." Divyansh looked at the sheet, four months of "later", and thought someone, probably him, had to talk to Mohit properly before this became a cold war.

qa.q: What did Mohit's line on the grocery sheet say for four months?
qa.a: It said "will pay later".

qa.q: What does Divyansh think needs to happen before things get worse?
qa.a: He feels someone, probably himself, should talk to Mohit properly before the hints turn into a cold war.

qa.q: Chirag chose a joke in front of everyone. What could Divyansh choose instead?
qa.a: Divyansh could sit with Mohit privately, show him the sheet and agree on when to settle up, which is clearer and kinder than public digs.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when everyone laughs except him?
qa.a: Mohit probably feels embarrassed and cornered, suddenly realising the flat has been quietly keeping score.

grounding: A flatmate notices one housemate never paying his share and sees the group quietly withdraw favours and make pointed jokes before anyone confronts him.

passage:
"Did you see? Nikhil took the umbrella again," Sarita said, pushing the door shut with her foot, grocery bags in both arms.
"Mine or yours?" Vijay asked.
"Yours. Mine's been missing since March."
"He also finished my coffee powder. Didn't replace it. Again."
Sarita dumped the bags. "I've stopped leaving him leftovers. Did you notice?"
"He noticed. He asked me why the fridge is so empty these days."
"What did you say?"
"I said, 'Funny, it fills up when people buy things.'" Vijay grinned, then stopped. "That was petty, na?"
"A bit. I've been petty too. I told Hina he's a freeloader."
Vijay sighed. "We're doing everything except talking to him."
"Tonight, then? Both of us. Calmly."
"Calmly," Vijay agreed. "After I buy more coffee powder."

qa.q: What did Nikhil finish and not replace?
qa.a: He finished Vijay's coffee powder and didn't replace it. Again.

qa.q: Why did Vijay stop grinning and ask "That was petty, na?"
qa.a: Vijay seemed uneasy, realising the pointed comment was a dig rather than an honest talk 😅

qa.q: What choice do Vijay and Sarita make at the end, and why is it better than what they've done so far?
qa.a: They decide to talk to Nikhil together, calmly, tonight, which is clearer than withheld leftovers, gossip and digs.

qa.q: How might Nikhil experience the last few weeks without anyone saying anything directly?
qa.a: Nikhil may feel the fridge and the mood cooling without understanding why, which could leave him confused or defensive.

grounding: Two flatmates notice a third who keeps taking and realise they have punished him with withdrawal, gossip and digs instead of talking to him.

passage: It was 7 pm, the office AC had switched off, and Tejas had his own client deck due by midnight. He'd already spent an hour helping the new intern, Rhea, untangle a spreadsheet, and hadn't minded; she'd been stuck, and she'd asked properly. Then Hrithik rolled his chair over. "Bro, can you just finish my summary slide? You're faster." It was the fourth time this month. Tejas remembered the Saturday he'd covered Hrithik's client call, and the cab fare Hrithik had never mentioned again. His stomach tightened; he hated saying no. He took a breath. "Not tonight, and honestly, not like this any more. I'm happy to help when you're stuck. But I've been doing your parts regularly, and it isn't working for me." Hrithik stared, then rolled back. Tejas opened his deck. His hands were a little shaky, and steady enough.

qa.q: How many times that month had Hrithik asked for help like this?
qa.a: It was the fourth time this month.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling as he took a breath before answering?
qa.a: His stomach tightened; he was nervous and hated saying no, yet he felt it had to be said 😰

qa.q: Why did Tejas's answer work better than simply saying "I'm busy"?
qa.a: He named the pattern calmly and left the door open for real need, so the limit was clear without being cruel.

qa.q: How might Rhea see Tejas, compared with how Hrithik sees him tonight?
qa.a: Rhea probably sees him as generous and patient, while Hrithik may feel suddenly cut off, even though he has received far more help.

grounding: A young professional helps an intern freely but calmly stops doing a colleague's work after a pattern of taking, despite his nerves.

passage: Gurleen's scooter keys hung by the door of her Chandigarh flat, and half the building knew it. She'd picked up Mrs Bedi's medicines from the chemist twice this week without being asked, and lent the scooter to the watchman's son for his college interview. She never kept track. Except with Nilesh from the second floor. He'd borrowed it nine times since Diwali, and it always came back on empty, once with a new scratch nobody explained. On Saturday he knocked again. "Keys, na? Just for an hour." Gurleen kept her hand on the door. "Nilesh, I'm going to stop lending you the scooter. It keeps coming back empty and you never mention it. I'm not angry. I'm just done." He laughed awkwardly. "Over petrol?" "Over the pattern," she said calmly, and closed the door gently.

qa.q: How many times had Nilesh borrowed the scooter since Diwali?
qa.a: He had borrowed it nine times since Diwali.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's "I'm not angry. I'm just done" show about her state of mind?
qa.a: She feels calm and settled rather than furious; she has decided and doesn't need a fight to hold the limit.

qa.q: What makes Gurleen's choice fair rather than stingy?
qa.a: She still helps freely with medicines and the interview, and stops only with the one person who takes without giving back, naming the reason plainly.

qa.q: Why might Nilesh laugh awkwardly and say "Over petrol?"
qa.a: Nilesh may feel caught out and embarrassed, trying to shrink the problem to petrol instead of facing the pattern she named.

grounding: A young adult who helps neighbours without counting calmly stops lending her scooter to one neighbour who habitually takes.

passage:
"Harsha, you're a lifesaver. Can I crash on your sofa again this weekend?" Gargi was already unzipping her bag.
"You stayed last weekend too."
"And the one before. But you don't mind, right?"
Harsha put the kettle on. "I didn't mind the first few times. When you lost the job, I was glad to help. I didn't want anything back."
"So...?"
"So since then it's been every weekend, and my grocery money, and you've never once asked how my week was."
Gargi stopped unzipping. "Wow. Okay."
"I'm not throwing you out tonight. Stay. But from next week, no more weekends here. If you're really stuck, tell me and we'll figure it out."
"You've been counting?"
"No. That's why it took me three months to notice."
Gargi was quiet. Then: "How was your week?"

qa.q: What did Gargi ask to do this weekend?
qa.a: Gargi asked to crash on Harsha's sofa again this weekend.

qa.q: What does Harsha's reply "That's why it took me three months to notice" reveal?
qa.a: It shows Harsha genuinely wasn't keeping score; the help was freely given, so the limit only came after a long pattern.

qa.q: Which parts of Harsha's choice kept it kind while still setting a limit?
qa.a: Harsha let Gargi stay tonight, left the door open for a real emergency, and spoke calmly about the pattern instead of blaming.

qa.q: What might be going on for Gargi when she finally asks "How was your week?"
qa.a: Gargi seems to realise, maybe with some embarrassment, that the friendship had become one-way, and tries to give something back.

grounding: A young adult who helped a friend generously calmly sets a limit once the friend keeps taking without giving back.

passage: Near the village school's water tank, four children were playing stapu on squares scratched into the mud. Dolma, five, stood at the edge holding her flat stone. "Can I play?" Anirban, drawing the last square, didn't look up. "No. You can't play with us. You're too small." Dolma didn't cry. She stood very still, stone in her fist, then sat on the steps, bent over. When the cook-didi rang the lunch bell, Dolma said, "My tummy hurts." Didi sat beside her and held her close. After a while she walked Dolma back and asked Anirban to show her how to throw.

qa.q: What were the four children playing near the water tank?
qa.a: They were playing stapu on squares scratched into the mud.

qa.q: What does Dolma's "My tummy hurts" suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests being left out hurt her like a real pain in her body, even though she didn't cry.

qa.q: What did the cook-didi do that helped?
qa.a: Didi sat close and held her, then asked Anirban to show Dolma how to throw, which gave Dolma a way back into the game.

qa.q: What might Anirban learn from being asked to teach Dolma the throw?
qa.a: Anirban might see that "too small" only means she needs showing, and notice how much the words hurt her.

grounding: A young child told she cannot play freezes and says her tummy hurts, showing exclusion felt as physical pain.

passage: In the park behind the nursery in Leeds, Freya and two other girls had squeezed into the wooden playhouse. Mina, five, ran over in yellow wellies. "Can I be the baby?" "No," said Freya, holding the door shut. "You can't play with us. It's full." Mina's face crumpled. She cried, then went quiet and pressed both hands on her stomach. When her mum came, Mina whispered, "My tummy hurts." Her mum knelt in the wet grass and asked what happened. Mina pointed at the playhouse. Her mum hugged her. "That hurt your feelings, and feelings can hurt in your tummy too." Then they fed the ducks together.

qa.q: What did Mina ask to be in the game?
qa.a: Mina asked, "Can I be the baby?"

qa.q: Why might Mina press both hands on her stomach after crying?
qa.a: Being shut out hurt so much that it felt like a real ache in her tummy.

qa.q: What did Mina's mum choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: She knelt, asked what happened, hugged Mina and named the hurt, so Mina felt believed and comforted.

qa.q: How might Freya see the playhouse moment?
qa.a: Freya may think she was only keeping the house from getting too full, without noticing how much her words hurt Mina.

grounding: A young child shut out of a game cries, goes quiet and says her tummy hurts, and her mother recognises the hurt as real.

passage: At the anganwadi, after the midday khichdi, the children built a train from plastic chairs. Wasim was the engine. Suraj, five, dragged over a chair. "I'm the last carriage." "No," said Wasim. "You can't play with us. You pushed yesterday." The chairs shuffled closer. Suraj froze, lips pressed tight. Later he told Kamla-tai his stomach was paining. She felt his forehead, then took him on her lap. "Did the train say no?" He nodded into her sari. Kamla-tai called Wasim over. "Suraj, can you say sorry for yesterday's push? And every train needs a guard." She gave Suraj her whistle.

qa.q: What did the children build after the midday khichdi?
qa.a: They built a train out of plastic chairs.

qa.q: What does Suraj freezing with lips pressed tight suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt shocked and hurt at being shut out, holding the pain in instead of crying.

qa.q: Which of Kamla-tai's choices helped Suraj back into the game?
qa.a: She took his stomach-ache seriously, guessed the real hurt, asked for a sorry about the push, and gave him a guard's role with a whistle.

qa.q: Why might Wasim have said no, and how might Wasim feel when Kamla-tai steps in?
qa.a: Wasim may still be upset about yesterday's push; hearing a sorry and staying the engine may make it easier to let Suraj join.

grounding: A young child told he cannot play freezes and complains of a stomach ache, and a caregiver treats the exclusion as a real hurt.

passage: It started on a Tuesday last month. I said "Good morning" to Ishita and she looked straight past me, like I was a window. At lunch, the four of them sat at the other end of the bench and talked in low voices. Nobody said anything mean. Nobody said anything at all. That was the worst part. If they'd teased me, at least I'd know what I did. I kept going over everything: the pencil I didn't return? The game I won? My stomach felt like it had a stone in it all day. That night Amma asked why I wasn't eating. I cried and told her. She sat with me and said, "Aditi, this isn't your fault. Tomorrow I'll talk to your class teacher." She did. It still took a week to feel normal again.

qa.q: What did Aditi say to Ishita on that Tuesday?
qa.a: Aditi said "Good morning", and Ishita looked straight past, like at a window.

qa.q: Why does Aditi say the silence was worse than teasing?
qa.a: With no words at all there was no clue about what went wrong, so Aditi felt confused and anxious, searching for a reason.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what made Amma's response helpful?
qa.a: The turning point was telling Amma; she listened, said it wasn't Aditi's fault, and spoke to the class teacher the next day.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel if she saw how much Aditi was hurting?
qa.a: Ishita might feel surprised or guilty, since ignoring someone can seem harmless to the person doing it.

grounding: A child whose friends suddenly stop speaking to them feels invisible, anxious and confused, finding the silence worse than teasing.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5C, Friday
For three days Nandini has been sitting alone during group work. Sunaina and the girls she usually sits with move their chairs when she comes near and talk to each other, never to her. No names, no teasing, just silence. Nandini asked me twice to go to the washroom during maths and came back with red eyes. Today she said, "Ma'am, am I invisible?" and laughed as if it were a joke. It wasn't.
What I did: I sat with Nandini at break and listened. She has no idea what she did. I told her it was not her fault and that I would help. I spoke with Sunaina separately; she said the group was "upset about the sleepover". I have called both families this evening, and on Monday the counsellor and I will sit with the girls together.

qa.q: What did Nandini ask the teacher today?
qa.a: Nandini asked, "Ma'am, am I invisible?" and laughed as if it were a joke.

qa.q: What do Nandini's red eyes and joking question suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: They suggest she feels hurt, anxious and confused, and is trying to hide how much the silence affects her.

qa.q: Which of the teacher's steps matter most, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with Nandini and saying it isn't her fault calms her right away, and talking to Sunaina and the families opens a way to find out what went wrong.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see the silence, given the comment about the sleepover?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel the group had a real grievance, without realising that silence hurts Nandini more than saying what upset them.

passage:
Wednesday
Day two of nobody talking to me. Ayesha passed the chalk box down the row and skipped me. Skipped me! Like my desk was empty. When I asked her about the science chart, she turned and asked Deepa what time it was. I didn't know that could hurt so much. I kept checking my bag for something I might have done wrong. Was it the birthday card? Did I talk too much at the picnic? I don't know, and not knowing makes my stomach flip over and over.
At dinner Paati asked why I was stirring my rasam and not drinking it. I told her everything. She didn't say "ignore them". She held my hand and said we'll tell Miss tomorrow, together, and that I haven't done anything to deserve silence.
I feel a bit lighter. Not much. A bit.
Kavitha

qa.q: What did Ayesha pass down the row?
qa.a: Ayesha passed the chalk box down the row and skipped Kavitha.

qa.q: What worry is making Kavitha's stomach flip over and over?
qa.a: Not knowing what went wrong; Kavitha keeps searching for a mistake, and the not-knowing fills Kavitha with worry.

qa.q: What choice at dinner changed how Kavitha felt?
qa.a: Kavitha chose to tell Paati everything, and Paati's hand, her plan to tell Miss together, and her reassurance made Kavitha feel a bit lighter.

qa.q: How might Paati feel hearing about the chalk box and the silence?
qa.a: Paati probably feels protective and sad, which is why she doesn't brush it off and plans to act the next day.

grounding: A child ignored by friends in class feels invisible and anxious about what they did wrong, and a grandmother responds with care.

passage: After the last bell, Tarun gathered the boys under the neem tree behind the panchayat school. "From tomorrow, nobody talks to Anand. Not in cricket, not on the bus." "Why?" asked little Bholu. "He told Sir we were playing in the storeroom. He's a snitch. He deserves it." Tarun said it loudly, and the others nodded one by one. Tarun felt tall, like the tree. Everyone was looking at him, waiting for the next rule. Last year it was Tarun who'd eaten lunch alone for a month after he dropped a catch in the final. He remembered the empty bench. He pushed the memory down. This time he was on the inside. Next morning, when Anand came smiling to the pitch, Tarun turned his back first, and the rest turned after him.

qa.q: Where did Tarun gather the boys?
qa.a: Under the neem tree behind the panchayat school.

qa.q: Why did Tarun push the memory of the empty bench down?
qa.a: Remembering how lonely it felt would make it harder to shut Anand out, and he wanted to stay on the inside, safe from being left out again.

qa.q: At the neem tree, what choice could Tarun have made instead of a freeze-out?
qa.a: He could have talked to Anand about the storeroom complaint directly, rather than turning a grudge into a rule for the whole group.

qa.q: What might it be like for Anand to walk onto the pitch smiling and see everyone turn their backs?
qa.a: Anand would likely feel shocked and confused, as lonely as Tarun once felt on the empty bench.

grounding: A child organises a group to shun a classmate, feeling powerful and safe from being left out himself, and tells himself the target deserves it.

passage: In the lunchroom of the school on Maple Street, Amara slid a folded note along the table: "Don't sit with Gabriel. Pass it on." It moved from hand to hand. When Gabriel came with his tray, the chairs next to Amara's group were suddenly saved. He stood there, then sat at the end near the bins. Amara laughed a little too loudly at something Chloe said. It felt good, everyone following her note. Safer, too. Last week Chloe had whispered with Lily all through art, and Amara had spent the whole lesson wondering if she'd be next. Now nobody would leave her out; she was the one deciding. Anyway, Gabriel had copied her maths answers once, she told herself. He probably deserved it. She didn't look at the bins end again.

qa.q: What did Amara's note say?
qa.a: "Don't sit with Gabriel. Pass it on."

qa.q: What was Amara afraid of before she started the note?
qa.a: After Chloe whispered with Lily all through art, Amara worried about being the next one left out.

qa.q: What could Amara do the next time she feels that fear, instead of passing a note?
qa.a: She could tell a friend or a teacher she felt left out in art, dealing with her own worry instead of pushing it onto Gabriel.

qa.q: What is lunch like for Gabriel, sitting near the bins?
qa.a: He probably feels humiliated and confused, not knowing why the chairs were suddenly saved.

grounding: A child leads a lunchroom freeze-out, enjoying the power and safety it gives her, driven by her own fear of being left out.

passage: At the Saturday badminton club, Devika had a plan. "When Manjula asks to be partners, everyone's already paired. Okay?" The other three nodded, and Devika felt a warm rush, like winning a long rally. Manjula came in with her new racquet and asked Priti, then Roshni, then Gulnaz. "Sorry, already paired." She ended up hitting the shuttle against the wall alone. Devika told herself it was fair. Manjula showed off, didn't she, always talking about her state-level cousin. Besides, if the group wasn't against Manjula, it might be against someone else, and Devika had heard Priti call her own backhand "weak". Better to be the one choosing. Then Coach Dias, watching from the net, called Devika over. "Why is one player at the wall every week?" Devika's warm feeling drained away.

qa.q: Who did Manjula ask to be partners before hitting against the wall?
qa.a: Manjula asked Priti, then Roshni, then Gulnaz.

qa.q: Why did Devika feel a warm rush when the others nodded?
qa.a: Having the group follow her plan made her feel powerful and safe, the one choosing rather than the one chosen against.

qa.q: Coach Dias's question is a turning point. What honest choice could Devika make in answering it?
qa.a: Devika could admit she set it up and why, including her fear about the backhand comment, and ask how to put it right with Manjula.

qa.q: What might Saturdays feel like for Manjula, hitting against the wall alone?
qa.a: Manjula probably feels embarrassed and lonely, bringing a new racquet only to find every partner already taken.

grounding: A child who organises a club freeze-out feels powerful, excuses it as deserved, and is partly driven by fear of being the target herself.

passage:
Thursday night
Noticed Binita again today. Third week she's eaten lunch on the steps by the library, earphones in, nothing playing (the wire wasn't even plugged in). She used to be all over our class group chat, and now when someone makes a plan, she's never tagged. I don't think anyone's being mean on purpose. People just forgot her, which is kind of worse.
So today I took my tiffin to the steps and sat two steps above, like I just wanted the shade. Asked her if she'd done the geography map. She had. Then I said, "Want to be in our group for the model? We need someone who can draw." She said, "Okay," very fast.
Didn't make a big deal. Nobody noticed. Good.
Tenzin

qa.q: Where has Binita been eating lunch for three weeks?
qa.a: On the steps by the library, earphones in, with nothing playing.

qa.q: Why does Tenzin think people forgetting Binita is "kind of worse"?
qa.a: Tenzin feels that meanness at least gets noticed, while quiet forgetting makes Binita invisible and nobody even sees the need to fix it.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin sit two steps above and ask about the geography map first?
qa.a: Tenzin chose a casual opening so it didn't look like a rescue, which let Binita say yes without feeling singled out.

qa.q: How might the invitation feel from Binita's side?
qa.a: After weeks of not being tagged, being asked because "we need someone who can draw" may feel like being wanted rather than pitied.

grounding: A classmate notices a student eating alone and left out of chats, and includes her in a group task without drawing attention.

passage: In the kasba school, the midday meal was served on the long verandah, and everyone ate in their usual rows. Parveen had noticed that for two weeks Imran, who'd joined when his father took a job at the dairy, sat at the far end by the tap, eating fast and leaving first. When teams formed for the Friday quiz, nobody called his name. Parveen didn't make a speech. On Monday she simply carried her plate to the tap end, "because the shade is better", and asked Imran if he'd got the last sum in the maths homework. He had. On Friday, when Sir told them to form quiz teams, she called out, "Imran's with us," before anyone else could choose. Nobody looked twice. Imran did, though, just once, and nodded.

qa.q: Where did Imran sit to eat his midday meal?
qa.a: At the far end of the verandah, by the tap.

qa.q: Why do you think Parveen said she moved "because the shade is better"?
qa.a: She wanted to sit with Imran without making it look like pity or drawing everyone's attention to him.

qa.q: Which of Parveen's small choices helped most on Friday, and why?
qa.a: Calling "Imran's with us" before teams formed made him part of the group naturally, so he wasn't left to be picked last.

qa.q: What might Imran's single nod say about how Parveen's actions felt to him?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed and was grateful, glad the welcome came quietly without anyone making a scene.

grounding: A classmate sees a new student eating alone and left out, and quietly sits with him and includes him in a team.

passage:
First week of October. Yamini found out from a photo: the five of them at the lake cafe, at the table she always sat at, with a caption about "the real ones". Nobody had told her. She sat on her hostel bed and let herself cry, then typed in her notes: "This hurts. It doesn't mean I'm unlovable."
Two weeks later. She messaged Ramesh from her lab group, the quiet one who always shared his charger: "Want to grab chai after practicals?" They talked about mosquitoes and question papers for an hour. She joined the Sunday cycling club too.
November. Someone from the old group posted about a party she wasn't invited to. Her thumb hovered over "leave group", then over a sharp reply. She did neither. She muted it and texted Ramesh about Sunday's ride.

qa.q: What did Yamini type in her notes?
qa.a: "This hurts. It doesn't mean I'm unlovable."

qa.q: What does Yamini's thumb hovering over a sharp reply suggest she was feeling in November?
qa.a: She still felt the sting and some urge to hit back, even after building new friendships.

qa.q: Which choice in November showed Yamini's recovery?
qa.a: She neither left angrily nor replied sharply; she muted the group and turned to Ramesh and the Sunday ride instead.

qa.q: How might Ramesh experience Yamini's invitation for chai?
qa.a: Ramesh, the quiet one in the lab group, may feel pleasantly noticed, so the new friendship matters to him too.

grounding: Over two months a young adult cut out of a friend group admits the hurt, builds new connections and resists striking back.

passage: Parul, beta, you think nobody has ever been dropped by their friends? When your Vasudha maasi was twenty-one, my whole group at the teachers' training college stopped calling me. One day I was sharing their lunch; the next day they had a new table and no seat for me. I never found out why. For weeks I thought something must be broken in me. Then one night I told myself: this hurts, and it is allowed to hurt, but it does not make me bad. I started eating with the two quiet girls from the science section, Farida and Rose. We are still friends; Rose sends me mangoes every summer. When one of the old group later came to me for notes, I gave them. I didn't want to become the thing that had hurt me. So cry today, beta. Tomorrow, find your Roses.

qa.q: What does Rose send Vasudha maasi every summer?
qa.a: Rose sends her mangoes every summer.

qa.q: What did young Vasudha believe about herself in the first weeks, and what changed?
qa.a: She thought something must be broken in her, until she told herself the hurt was allowed but did not make her bad.

qa.q: Why did giving notes to someone from the old group matter to Vasudha maasi?
qa.a: It was a choice not to shut someone out in return, so she wouldn't become the thing that had hurt her.

qa.q: What might Parul take from "find your Roses"?
qa.a: Parul might see that today's pain is real but that new, accepting friends can be found, as Vasudha maasi found Farida and Rose.

grounding: An elder recalls being dropped by her college group, admitting the hurt, finding new friends and refusing to exclude in return.

passage: The rain had knocked out the PG's power for the third night, and Jyoti was revising for her final exam by phone torch when she saw it: her four roommates had made a new chat for the farewell trip, and she wasn't in it. The kettle was dead, her battery was at twelve percent, and the exam was at nine. She let herself feel it for a minute, face in the pillow. Then she typed to her mother: "Feeling left out today. I'm okay, just sad." Her mother replied, "Call me after the exam." Next she messaged Rehana from her tutorial class: "Revising Paper 6? Library tomorrow after the exam?" Rehana said yes. Jyoti thought about sending her roommates a cold "enjoy your trip". She didn't. She plugged in the power bank and opened her notes.

qa.q: What was Jyoti's phone battery at when she saw the new chat?
qa.a: Her battery was at twelve percent.

qa.q: What does "Feeling left out today. I'm okay, just sad" show about how Jyoti is handling it?
qa.a: She admits the hurt honestly without deciding it means something is wrong with her.

qa.q: What choice did Jyoti make about the "enjoy your trip" message, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She didn't send it; striking back would have fed the coldness, while messaging Rehana and her mother gave her real support.

qa.q: How might Rehana experience the library invitation?
qa.a: Rehana might simply see a classmate wanting a study partner, and a new friendship could grow from it without any backstory.

grounding: On a hard night before an exam, a young adult left out by roommates admits the hurt, reaches out to others and does not retaliate.
